To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

ML technologies can be applied to a wide variety of tasks, that the tasks that ML can perform are not necessarily the same ones that humans can perform, and that the SML of tasks varies greatly across occupations and job categories.
ML technologies will be used to automate many types of work, but the extent of ML use in a given job category is highly variable.

(1) ML technologies will grow more pervasive, (2) the SML of tasks varies greatly, (3) the SML rubric can serve as a predictor for the reorganization of a given job, and (4) the reorganization of jobs can be a source of job creation and destruction.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how ML is likely to affect work and the labor market in the future.
the question of how ML is changing the nature of work and what the implications are for the economy and society.
the potential impact of machine learning on jobs and occupations.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
ML technologies will not eliminate jobs in the near term.
the SML of work activities varies greatly, and that ML technologies will grow more pervasive, and will likely lead to reorganization and redefinition of jobs and occupations.
the SML of a job or occupation is a useful indicator to understand the extent to which ML technologies can replace human work.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
ML will be a disruptive force for the future of work, but its impact will vary greatly depending on the nature of the task.
ML will be more prevalent in the future, but the extent to which it will be applied will depend on the tasks performed by workers.
we have developed a rubric that can help to assess the suitability of ML in a particular job and to identify potential reorganization of work tasks within an occupation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ML technologies can be applied to tasks in a variety of occupations and that the impact of ML on jobs and occupations is likely to be more nuanced than the popular narrative of “robots taking over.”
the impact of ML on the economy will depend on the nature of the work tasks, and not on whether a job title contains the word “driver,” “writer,” “doctor,” or “lawyer.”
the potential for ML to replace work activities varies greatly across occupations and that, in many instances, the potential for ML will be limited.
